paper_a.title: XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System

paper_b.title: Greedy Function Approximation: A Gradient Boosting Machine

metadata.description: XGBoost (Chen-Guestrin 2016) extends Friedman's Gradient Boosting Machine (1999/2001) along the gradient-boosting skeleton: same additive tree expansion and stagewise greedy fitting, but with explicit L1/L2-style regularization (gamma T + lambda |w|^2), a second-order Taylor approximation that uses Hessian information h_i in addition to the gradient g_i, a closed-form structure score and split gain derived from this approximation, a weighted-quantile sketch with proven approximation guarantees for distributed approximate split finding, a sparsity-aware split algorithm with default directions, and engineering contributions (column blocks, cache-aware access, out-of-core blocks). Friedman's paper provides the conceptual scaffolding (function-space steepest descent, generic Gradient Boost, LS/LAD/M/L2/LK TreeBoost specializations) that XGBoost's more general regularized objective subsumes. Note paper B is PDF-fallback (reduced math fidelity).

matches.explanation: Both pose the supervised function-estimation problem: minimize an empirical loss over an additive expansion of base learners. XGBoost's problem (ProbP271.1) adds an explicit regularizer Omega(f_k) on per-tree complexity, while Friedman's (ProbP272.1) is the unregularized expected-loss minimization. Same role (defines the optimization target the rest of the paper attacks), different formulation (regularized vs. unregularized; finite sample sum vs. expectation).

Tree Ensemble Model (DP271.1) is the additive expansion specialized to CART regression trees with leaf-weight maps w_{q(x)}. Friedman's Additive Expansion (DP272.1) is the more general additive form sum beta_m h(x; a_m) over arbitrary base learners. Same conceptual role (the function class being optimized over); XGBoost commits to trees from the outset where Friedman keeps h generic.

XGBoost's Regularized Learning Objective (Omega(f) = gamma T + (1/2) lambda ||w||^2) has no direct counterpart in Friedman 1999. Friedman's regularization is implicit (early stopping, shrinkage nu) rather than an explicit penalty term per tree. This is a paper-A contribution that defines the EXT direction.

XGBoost's gradient statistics g_i and h_i (DP271.4) include both first AND second derivatives of the loss at the previous iterate. Friedman's function-space steepest descent (DP272.4) uses only the first-order gradient g_m(x). The paper-A definition is the natural second-order extension: g_i is the same object; h_i is new. This is the key analytic upgrade behind XGBoost's closed-form structure score.

XGBoost's second-order Taylor expansion of the boosting objective (EP271.1: g_i f_t + (1/2) h_i f_t^2 + Omega) replaces Friedman's first-order linearization (DP272.4) and stagewise fit (DP272.5). Both reduce the per-iteration sub-problem to a tractable surrogate, but XGBoost's quadratic surrogate admits a closed-form optimum where Friedman's linear surrogate requires fitting a least-squares regression to pseudo-residuals plus a separate line search.

XGBoost rewrites its objective as a weighted least-squares regression with weight h_i and target g_i/h_i (EP271.5). Friedman's Constrained Negative Gradient (DP272.6) fits the base learner to the unweighted negative gradient -g_m(x_i) via least squares. Both reduce base-learner fitting to a (weighted) LS problem; the weights h_i are the second-order extension.

Optimal leaf weight (EP271.2) and structure score (EP271.3) are XGBoost-original closed-form formulas that follow from the second-order objective and L2 leaf-weight regularization. Friedman has no analog: his terminal-node updates (gamma_lm) are loss-specific Newton or median formulas (e.g. AP272.5's gamma_klm = sum y_tilde / sum |y_tilde|(2-|y_tilde|)), not derived from a unified regularized quadratic surrogate.

XGBoost's split-gain formula (EP271.4) and the explicit best-split-finding problem (ProbP271.2) are paper-A contributions specific to the regularized second-order objective. Friedman uses standard CART split criteria implicitly inside his tree base learner but never formalizes a problem statement or writes a closed-form gain formula tied to his stagewise loss.

Both are the core split-finding/base-learner-fitting algorithm of their respective methods. AP272.1 (Gradient Boost) is Friedman's generic stagewise procedure: compute pseudo-responses y_tilde_i = -g_m(x_i), fit base learner to them via least squares, line-search rho_m, update F_m. AP271.1 (Exact Greedy Split Finding) is the analogous tree-construction inner loop in XGBoost, but for one tree it directly maximizes the second-order split gain over all features and thresholds rather than fitting a residual. Same role at different abstraction levels; XGBoost replaces the LS-fit + line-search of Gradient Boost with a single closed-form gain optimization.

LS Boost (AP272.2) instantiates Gradient Boost with squared error, fitting the residual y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i). XGBoost's Exact Greedy (AP271.1) under the squared-error loss with lambda = gamma = 0 reduces to greedily growing a single regression tree to the residuals, mirroring the inner step of LS Boost. The explicit second-order machinery becomes trivial in this special case.

Approximate Algorithm for Split Finding (AP271.2) using percentile-based bucketing of features per tree (global) or per split (local) is an XGBoost engineering contribution to handle large/distributed data. Friedman 1999 has no histogram-based approximate split finding and no distributed setting.

Sparsity-aware Split Finding (AP271.3) with learned default directions for missing/zero entries is a paper-A original. Friedman addresses neither sparse data structure nor missing-value handling within tree splits.

The entire weighted-quantile-sketch theoretical contribution of XGBoost (sketch algorithm AP271.5, query function AP271.4, definitions of weighted rank function DP271.5, quantile summary DP271.6 with extension DP271.7 and epsilon-approximation DP271.8, problem statement ProbP271.3, equation EP271.6, theorems TP271.1/TP271.2 on merge and prune, and supporting lemmas LP271.1-LP271.4 with their proofs PP271.1-PP271.5) has no counterpart in Friedman 1999. Friedman does not consider quantile sketching, weighted streaming, or distributed data structures. This is the paper's main theoretical novelty over GBM.

Column block (CSC) data structure (DP271.9) and its time-complexity proposition (PrP271.1) are systems-level contributions of XGBoost with no Friedman analog. Friedman discusses asymptotic linear scaling in N, n, M (RP272.3) only at the high level of after-sorting CART, not via a per-iteration cached column-block structure.

XGBoost's Shrinkage remark (RP271.1: scale newly added weights by eta) is mathematically the same as Friedman's Proportional Shrinkage Regularization (DP272.8: F_m = F_{m-1} + nu * rho_m h(x, a_m)). XGBoost cites this directly as borrowed from Friedman. Names differ (eta vs nu) but the construction is identical.

XGBoost's external citation to Gradient Tree Boosting (AP271.6, origin: external, citing Friedman 2001) is exactly Friedman's Gradient Boost algorithm (AP272.1). This is the explicit external-vs-paper-origin link establishing the EXT relation: paper A cites paper B as its conceptual precursor.

GK Quantile Summary theorem (TP271.3) is cited from Greenwald-Khanna and Zhang-Wang, not from Friedman; included here only because it has origin: external. Skipping per the origin-aware filtering rules.

Friedman's loss-specific TreeBoost specializations (LAD AP272.3 for |y-F|, M AP272.4 for Huber, L2 AP272.5 for two-class logistic, LK AP272.6 for K-class logistic) all instantiate the generic Gradient Boost with loss-specific pseudo-responses and Newton-like terminal-node updates. XGBoost's split-finding family (exact AP271.1, approximate AP271.2, sparsity-aware AP271.3) is loss-agnostic by design: any twice-differentiable loss feeds into g_i, h_i and the same algorithms run. Cross-paper, the relationship is many-to-many: XGBoost subsumes Friedman's per-loss algorithms via its second-order surrogate. Confidence low because the alignment is conceptual rather than statement-level.

Friedman's Common Loss Functions (DP272.2: squared error, absolute error, neg log-likelihood) is enumerated to drive the loss-specific TreeBoost variants. XGBoost works with any twice-differentiable loss generically and does not enumerate canonical losses in its definitions; the role is dissolved into the general g_i, h_i framework.

Steepest-Descent Increments (DP272.3) is paper-B's parameter-space gradient-descent setup, marked origin external (classical numerical optimization) and used to motivate function-space steepest descent. No XGBoost counterpart; skipping per origin filtering would also justify omission, but listing for completeness on the paper-B side.

Influence Trimming (DP272.7) is a Friedman-original acceleration technique for L2 / LK TreeBoost (delete observations with very small weights w_i below an alpha-quantile). XGBoost has no analog; it relies on column-block sorting, cache-awareness, and out-of-core IO instead.

ANOVA Functional Decomposition (DP272.9, marked external) and its companion claim that L-terminal-node trees produce interaction order min(L-1, n) (ClP272.1) are paper-B-original interpretability/structural commentary. XGBoost makes no such interaction-order argument.

The interpretability machinery of GBM (continuous and tree-based relative influence DP272.10/DP272.11, partial dependence DP272.12 and its weighted tree-traversal AP272.7, the LS split improvement formula EP272.1, the linear-target justification claim ClP272.2, and the marginal-vs-conditional remark RP272.1) is a paper-B contribution with no counterpart in XGBoost. XGBoost focuses on training scalability, not post-hoc model interpretation.

Friedman's invariance/robustness remark (RP272.2) and computational scaling remark (RP272.3) are paper-B-specific summarizing observations. XGBoost's complexity discussion (PrP271.1) addresses related territory but with very different emphasis (column blocks, Klog n -> K factor); not paired here to avoid over-aligning.
